member.name: PrecededByPunctuation
member.para: What actually precedes an announcement. Measured 2026-08-28 over the Perry Rhodan Silber-Edition library (159 books, build 411 debug logs), counting every "Kapitel N" appearing anywhere in a transcript segment - 31,294 readings. 31,006 of them (99.1%) open their segment and were already covered by the segment-start route. Of the rest, all of which sit mid-segment behind whitespace: 152 follow a comma, 31 a full stop, 6 a hyphen, and 94 follow a letter or a digit. That last group is the one that must stay out - it is narration ("Der erste Kapitel 5"), and requiring whitespace plus punctuation excludes every one of them.

What the route is worth, and what it costs. Restricted to the window transcripts whose match actually reaches AnnouncementIsolation.ForChapter - so excluding the refinement's own short probes, which routinely do give the announcement a segment of its own without that ever reaching the guard - 16 chapter positions across the library were heard only behind punctuation. 13 of them were marked anyway, another window having opened a segment for them. Exactly 3 were newly admitted, and they are exactly the 3 chapters the library lost: "Der Loower und das Auge" 14 (0.70 s of lead-in), "Die Ewigen Diener" 23 (0.58 s) and "Die Gravo-Katastrophe" 25 (0.64 s), each announced as "<Schauplatz>, Kapitel N" and each discarded for want of the 0.85 s the pause route asks. Zero false positives. A fourth, "Laire" 16 (0.83 s), had been discarded and then recovered 20 s later by a re-read that framed the announcement differently - the evidence that the margin here is knife-edge rather than categorical.

Why the whitespace is required rather than assumed. Five of the library's readings have the announcement glued straight onto the character before it with no space. Admitting those would mean admitting a chapter word that is the tail of another token, which is the shape the lead-in guard exists to reject - the Italian "riepilogo" case in notes\Detection\AnnouncementIsolation.xml is the same shape one level down, inside a word.

member.name: CarriesWords
member.para: How common the tags are. Counted over the sixteen books of the L:\Temp corpus (2026-08-09): "[Musik]" 259x, "[Abspann]" 130x, "[BLANK_AUDIO]" 103x, "[Aufregende Musik]" 57x, "[MUSIK]" 38x, "[Musica]" 24x, in 14 of the 16. The spread across languages and spellings is what rules out matching a word list.

Both defects are real in mechanism and neither has cost anything yet (re-measured 2026-08-20 over the seventeen frozen build-366 logs; scratchpad\tags.py). Of 10,298 logged transcripts 35 are nothing but tags - the shape that vetoes , up from 9 of 5,800 when this was first counted at build 280. Of 4,555 "no" answers from an onset or survival probe, 30 open with a tag and only 3 have real words behind it - all three in "Das Mutantenkorps", and all three ordinary narration ("Als ich die ersten Sonnenbewerber habe,", "Eine solche Geschäftigkeit"), so every one of those "no" answers was right. That is the same verdict the build-280 count reached on different data, which is why this shipped as a correctness tidy-up rather than as a fix for an observed loss.

Provably inert on the corpus, which is the safety argument. For the 27 tag-only "no" answers, discounting the tag leaves the probe no segment at all and the answer stays "no"; for the 3 with narration behind it, the probe now reads the narration, which is not the phrase, and the answer stays "no". So no mark can move on this corpus. Where it does change behaviour - a jingle window whose only "speech" was a tag - the re-read it unblocks keeps the window's own bounds and can only add a mark, never move one, the same safety shape as the other empty-window fallbacks.

Only 216 tag segments appear in the whole build-366 corpus and every one is a single bracketed run - no segment holds two. The regex is written for that single-run shape accordingly; widen it only against a counter-example.
